title: The Interpreter
author: Tadoku Note (original)
summary: ベテラン医療通訳のミナコは、病院で日本人旅行者の老夫婦を担当します。正確に訳すことと、人に寄り添うこと。その間で彼女が選んだ言葉とは。

source.note: Original text written for this app.

paragraphs: Minako Hayes had been a medical interpreter at St. Columba’s Hospital in Boston for nineteen years, and in that time she had learned that the most important words in any language were usually the shortest ones. “Yes.” “No.” “Pain.” “Here.” “Why?” She had interpreted for broken arms and difficult births, for heart attacks and car accidents, for good news so sudden that families laughed and wept at the same time. She was good at her job because she had trained herself, over many years, to become invisible: a voice and nothing more, a clear glass window between two people who could not otherwise see each other.

That, at least, was the theory. The professional code of ethics she had signed was very clear. Interpret everything. Add nothing. Omit nothing. Do not give advice. Do not take sides. Do not let your own feelings shape the message.

The call came at four in the afternoon on a wet Thursday in November. A Japanese tourist, a man in his late seventies, had collapsed in the lobby of a hotel near the harbor. His wife was with him. Neither of them spoke more than a few words of English.

Minako found the wife sitting very straight on a plastic chair outside the emergency department, her handbag held tightly on her knees, as if somebody might try to take it from her. She was small and neatly dressed, with gray hair cut short, and she was looking at the floor.
“Mrs. Ota?” Minako said gently in Japanese. “My name is Hayes. I am an interpreter. I will be with you while you talk to the doctors.”
The woman looked up, and for a moment her face simply collapsed with relief. Then she recovered herself, stood up and bowed deeply. “I am sorry to trouble you,” she said. “Thank you very much.”

Her name was Teruko. Her husband was Shigeo. They had been married for fifty-one years. This was their first trip abroad together. Their daughter had arranged everything, a week in Boston and New York, as a present for their golden wedding anniversary, which they had been too busy to celebrate the year before. Shigeo had wanted to see the ocean from the other side. He had been a fisherman in a small town in Miyagi, Teruko explained, until the tsunami in 2011 took the boat, the harbor and most of the town. After that, he had worked in a factory. He had never complained.

The doctor who came out to speak to them was young, perhaps thirty, with tired eyes and a careful manner. Her name was Dr. Alvarez. She sat down next to Teruko, which Minako noticed and appreciated; many doctors spoke standing up.

“Your husband has had a major stroke,” Dr. Alvarez said. “There was bleeding inside his brain. We have stabilized him for now, but the damage is very serious. I’m afraid I need to be honest with you. It is very unlikely that he will wake up. And if he does, he will not be the same person. We need to talk about what he would want.”

Minako interpreted. She chose each word with precision. She did not soften the message, and she did not make it harsher. She watched Teruko’s face as the meaning reached her, and she saw the small, terrible moment when hope stops.

Teruko was silent for a long time. Then she asked a question that Minako had heard, in different forms, perhaps a hundred times. “Is it because of me? I should have noticed. This morning he said his head felt heavy. I told him it was the long flight. I told him to drink water.”
Minako interpreted the question into English. Dr. Alvarez shook her head firmly. “No. Please tell her no. Nothing she could have done this morning would have changed this.”
Minako interpreted that too, word for word. Teruko nodded, but Minako could see that she did not believe it. Not yet.

Over the next two days, Minako was called back to the hospital again and again. There were consent forms, conversations with a neurologist, calls to the daughter in Sendai, who was trying desperately to get a flight. There were questions about insurance, about the hotel, about what happened to a person’s body if they died far from home. Through all of it, Teruko remained calm and polite, apologizing constantly for the trouble she was causing. She slept in a chair beside her husband’s bed. She did not cry, at least not where anyone could see.

On the second evening, the doctors gathered for what they called a family meeting. Shigeo’s condition had become worse. Machines were now breathing for him. The team needed to discuss whether to continue that support. The daughter joined by video from an airport in Tokyo, her face pale and blurred on the screen of Minako’s tablet.

Dr. Alvarez explained the situation slowly and carefully. Minako interpreted every sentence. The daughter asked practical questions, and Minako interpreted those. Then Teruko spoke. She did not speak to the doctor. She looked at Minako.
“May I ask you something?” she said quietly. “Not the doctor. You.”
Minako felt the familiar boundary rise inside her like a wall. Her training was clear. Everything that was said in the room must be interpreted. She was not a participant. She was a window.
“I must interpret anything you say to me,” Minako said gently. “That is my job. Do you still want to ask?”

Teruko nodded. “Then please interpret it. I want the doctor to hear it too.” She took a breath. “My husband lost his boat, his town, his brother and most of his friends in one afternoon. After that, he lived for thirteen more years. Every morning, he walked to the sea and looked at it, even though the sea took everything. I asked him once why he did that. He said, ‘Because it is beautiful, and it is not the sea’s fault.’ Yesterday, before he fell, we stood in front of the hotel and looked at the harbor here. He said, ‘Now I have seen the same sea from both sides. That is enough.’” She stopped. “I want to know if it is wrong for me to think that he was ready.”

Minako turned to Dr. Alvarez and began to interpret. She had done this thousands of times. But this time she found it unexpectedly difficult. The problem was one small phrase. In Japanese, Shigeo had said “mō jūbun da.” Literally, it meant “That is already enough.” But in his voice, in that moment, according to his wife, it had not meant resignation. It had meant something closer to completeness. Satisfaction. A circle closing.

Minako had a choice. She could translate the words literally: “That is enough.” It would be accurate. No supervisor could criticize it. But she knew how it would sound in English to an American doctor: tired, defeated, perhaps even depressed. It might suggest that Shigeo had given up on life. That was not what his wife was saying.
She thought for one second, which felt much longer.

“He said, ‘Now I have seen the same sea from both sides,’” Minako interpreted. “And then he said something that literally means ‘That is enough.’ But I need to add, as the interpreter, that in Japanese, in this context, the phrase does not sound sad. It means something like ‘My life is complete. I am satisfied.’ I want to be sure that the meaning is clear.”

This was allowed. She knew that. An interpreter could step forward to explain a cultural or linguistic point, as long as she said clearly that she was doing so, and then returned to her role. But it was the first time in years that she had felt the weight of such a decision.

Dr. Alvarez listened, and her face softened. She turned to Teruko and spoke directly to her, as she had been trained to do, while Minako interpreted. “Mrs. Ota, it isn’t wrong. It sounds like you knew your husband very well. And it sounds like he told you something important. When we make decisions now, we try to make the decision he would make, if he could speak. You are helping him speak.”

Teruko listened to the interpretation. Then, for the first time, she cried. It was not dramatic. Her shoulders shook a little, and she held her handkerchief to her face, and she said, over and over, very quietly, “Thank you. Thank you.” Minako did not know whether she was speaking to the doctor, to Minako, or to her husband.

The daughter arrived the next morning. That afternoon, with both of them beside him, holding his hands, the machines were turned off. Shigeo Ota died a little after five o’clock, as the lights of the harbor were coming on outside the window.
Minako was not in the room. Interpreters often were not, at the end. It was not a moment that needed language.

A month later, a small package arrived for her at the hospital, with a Japanese stamp. Inside was a letter in careful handwriting and a photograph. In the photo, an elderly couple stood side by side in front of a gray harbor, under a cloudy sky, in matching blue raincoats. They were not smiling. They looked, Minako thought, entirely at peace.
“Dear Ms. Hayes,” the letter said. “Thank you for carrying my husband’s words across the sea. You carried them exactly as he meant them. I am sure it was not easy.”

Minako kept the letter in her desk drawer for the rest of her career. She never again thought of herself as a window. A window, she had realized, only lets light through. An interpreter has to know what the light means.
